title: Responses of multi‐year plant–pollinator networks to temperature and drought variation across continents
content:
This study brings together 12 multi-year plant–pollinator networks across four continents to test how temperature and drought shape ecological communities. Climate influenced species composition and interactions, but responses varied strongly among systems, while overall network structure remained surprisingly stable, revealing which aspects of plant–pollinator communities are most sensitive to climatic variation.


Abstract

Climate change is shifting species' distributions, activity periods and abundances, with consequences for species and interactions. Plant–pollinator interactions play a crucial role in maintaining biodiversity and ecosystem functioning, but it remains unclear whether responses to climatic variation are consistent across systems or depend on local ecological context. Here, we synthesize 12 multi-year plant–pollinator network datasets from four continents to examine how interannual variation in temperature and drought shapes pollinator assemblages, floral resources and their interactions. Specifically, we ask how (Q1) pollinator and floral richness and evenness, (Q2) community composition and (Q3) network structure respond to temperature and drought anomalies (deviations from the 1950–1990 baseline climate). Pollinator richness declined with drought, but also with wetter anomalies, exhibiting a hump-shaped response. Floral richness tended to decrease with increasing temperature, but had no detectable response to drought. Pollinator evenness showed no relationship with drought anomalies and decreased with increasing temperature anomalies, whereas plant evenness was positively related to wetter conditions. Community composition varied substantially among years within study sites, with pollinator assemblages exhibiting higher temporal turnover than floral assemblages. However, relationships between climatic anomalies and community composition varied among systems, with climate–composition relationships detected only at a subset of sites. Network structure showed limited responses to climatic variation. Connectance, nestedness and network-level specialization (H 2′) showed no detectable relationships with climatic anomalies, whereas interaction evenness increased under wetter conditions and declined under warmer conditions. Species-level specialization (d′) decreased under wetter and warmer conditions, suggesting greater interaction generalization under those conditions. Overall, climatic anomalies influenced multiple aspects of plant–pollinator communities and interactions, but responses varied substantially across sites and levels of ecological organization. Community composition and several species- and interaction-level properties responded to interannual climatic variation, whereas emergent network-level properties remained comparatively stable despite substantial temporal turnover within sites. Exploratory comparisons among sites suggested that climatic context, seasonality and sampling structure may contribute to this heterogeneity. Our findings highlight the importance of long-term ecological network studies and cross-system datasets for understanding how climate shapes ecological communities and species interactions under ongoing climate change.
